10.1002_adma.75052: Aqueous Zn metal batteries (AZMBs) are promising candidates for next‐generation energy storage due to their low cost and high safety. However, uncontrolled Zn dendrite growth under high current densities remains a critical challenge. Solvation structure engineering shows considerable potential in mitigating dendrite formation, but its effectiveness under realistic electric field conditions remains to be fully understood. In this work, we applied in situ extended x‐ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) spectroscopy and in situ Raman spectroscopy to directly probe the solvation behavior of Zn 2+ under an applied electric field. By introducing a cost‐effective electrolyte additive, we achieve a responsive “dynamic solvation structure” that adapts to rapid charge/discharge conditions, enhancing Zn stripping kinetics and promoting reversible Zn deposition. In situ and ex situ characterization techniques reveal that the additive effectively reduces polarization, suppresses inactive Zn accumulation, and facilitates fast charge transfer at the solid/electrolyte interface, significantly improving Zn cycling stability. As a result, our strategy demonstrates outstanding electrochemical performance, delivering a 650 mAh Zn─I 2 pouch cell with a high‐utilization Zn anode (50%) and high‐loading cathode for 300 cycles. This study presents a novel approach for optimizing Zn 2 + solvation dynamics, thereby paving the way for high‐performance AZMBs.
10.1002_aenm.202504572: 2D/3D perovskite heterostructures have advanced the performance of perovskite solar cells. However, ion diffusion at the 2D/3D interface under illumination and prolonged heat affects device stability and scalability. Here, we studied the electron‐withdrawing strength of aromatic ammonium ligand on perovskite interface stability. We tuned the electron‐withdrawing strength of the ligand through the incorporation of oxygen atoms on heterocyclic rings, and found that the ligand possessing the strongest electron‐withdrawing capability effectively suppresses 2D formation while preventing cation interdiffusion and maximizing defect passivation, outperforming conventional 2D/3D strategies. Consequently, we achieved power conversion efficiencies of 26.1% in 0.16 cm 2 lab‐scale cells and 19.1% in 809 cm 2 industrial‐scale solar modules. These encapsulated modules exhibited excellent damp‐heat (85°C/85% relative humidity) stability and operational durability, with <10% efficiency loss after 2500 and 3000 h, respectively. Moreover, the modules maintained steady power output over 30 days of outdoor operation, underscoring their potential for practical real‐world applications.
10.1002_aenm.71799: During the start‐up/shut‐down (SU/SD) processes of proton‐exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs), anode reversal generates an excessively high voltage that accelerates corrosion of the cathode Pt/C catalyst. Conventional approaches focus on blocking the delivery of oxygen or electrons to the anode, but fail to address the intrinsic activity coupling of Pt/C for both hydrogen oxidation reaction (HOR) and oxygen reduction reaction (ORR). Here, we report a strategy that can selectively tailor the catalytic function of Pt nanoparticles. We used phosphorus to modulate the electronic structure of low‐loading Pt clusters on a carbon support, forming a Pt/P‐BP catalyst. The P‐coordination downshifts the d ‐band center of Pt cluster, as evidenced by in situ ATR‑FTIR spectroscopy and DFT calculations, thereby widening the activity gap between HOR and ORR. Specifically, compared to Pt/C, Pt/P‐BP enhances HOR mass activity by fivefold while substantially suppressing ORR, transforming Pt from a bifunctional catalyst into a highly selective HOR catalyst. Consequently, Pt/P‐BP achieves a 10.8‐fold higher HOR/ORR selectivity than Pt/C. In SU/SD experiments, the Pt/P‐BP anode significantly reduces carbon corrosion of the cathode catalyst layer, maintaining the fuel cell performance better than Pt/C. This work paves a new avenue toward durable PEMFCs and inspires the selectivity design for electrocatalysts.
10.1021_acs.analchem.6c03876: Gel electromembrane extraction (G-EME) using agarose gel membranes is a green and effective approach for the selective transport of ionic analytes. However, its application is often limited by electroendosmotic flow (EEO) and the poor mechanical stability of agarose hydrogel membranes, particularly when combined with an organic solvent-based protein removal method for protein-rich samples. In this work, an electric-field-induced integration of selective ionic transport and protein electrocoagulation is introduced using a thin-film xerogel that combines electromembrane extraction and protein electrocoagulation into a single analytical step. Conversion of the hydrogel into a xerogel produces a mechanically robust, low-water-content membrane with reduced thickness, which suppresses EEO while still allowing efficient electromigration of charged analytes. The improved stability of the xerogel membrane permits operation at elevated electric fields sufficient to induce in situ protein electrocoagulation, thereby disrupting protein−drug binding and providing simultaneous matrix cleanup during extraction. The developed method offers a broad linear range (1−100 ng mL−1), acceptable precision (<11% (intra-day) and <12% (inter-day)), low limits of detection (0.3 ng mL−1), low limit of quantification (1 ng mL−1), extraction efficiency up to 88%, and enrichment factor up to 44. Norfloxacin and ciprofloxacin were extracted directly from milk samples and quantified by HPLC-UV with an accuracy of 78−110%. These results demonstrate that a thin-film agarose xerogel membrane provides a simple and effective platform for suppressing EEO and integrating extraction with electrocoagulation, enabling robust EME of antibiotics from protein-rich food matrices.
